section.title: Preparations to Build the Temple
section.sectionRationale: Before a single stone of the temple is laid, Solomon must gather materials and skill he does not have at home. He conscripts a workforce, writes to Hiram king of Tyre for cedar, craftsmen, and provisions, and Hiram replies with a blessing and the promised help. The chapter is entirely preparation, yet it already confesses the theology that will govern the whole project: the house is not a container for God but a place to burn sacrifice before a God too great for heaven itself to hold.
section.thesis: Solomon's careful, humble preparations, admitting that no house could ever contain the God of heaven, show that the temple was conceived from the outset not as a cage for deity but as a place of sacrifice and prayer, built with willing help even from a foreign king who blesses the God of Israel.
section.frameNote: Three beats: Solomon's purpose and workforce, verses 1 to 2; his message to Hiram confessing God's greatness and requesting materials, verses 3 to 10; and Hiram's reply, provision, and the numbering of the workforce, verses 11 to 18.

units.label: Solomon's purpose and workforce
units.note: a house for the Name of the LORD

verses.text: Now Solomon purposed to build a {{bayit|house}} for the {{shem|Name}} of the LORD and a royal palace for himself.
So he conscripted 70,000 porters, 80,000 stonecutters in the mountains, and 3,600 supervisors.

units.label: Solomon's message to Hiram
units.note: who can build Him a house

verses.text: Then Solomon sent word to Hiram king of Tyre: "Do for me as you did for my father David when you sent him cedars to build himself a house to live in.

Behold, I am about to build a house for the Name of the LORD my God to dedicate to Him for burning fragrant incense before Him, for displaying the showbread continuously, and for making burnt offerings every morning and evening as well as on the Sabbaths, New Moons, and appointed feasts of the LORD our God. This is ordained for Israel forever.
The house that I am building will be great, for our God is greater than all gods.

But who is able to build a house for Him, since the {{shamayim|heavens}}, even the highest heavens, cannot contain Him? Who then am I, that I should build a house for Him, except as a place to burn sacrifices before Him?

Send me, therefore, a craftsman skilled in engraving to work with gold and silver, with bronze and iron, and with purple, crimson, and blue yarn. He will work with my craftsmen in Judah and Jerusalem, whom my father David provided.
Send me also cedar, cypress, and algum logs from Lebanon, for I know that your servants have skill to cut timber there. And indeed, my servants will work with yours
to prepare for me timber in abundance, because the temple I am building will be great and wonderful.
I will pay your servants, the woodcutters, 20,000 cors of ground wheat, 20,000 cors of barley, 20,000 baths of wine, and 20,000 baths of olive oil."

units.label: Hiram's reply and the workforce numbered
units.note: a skillful man, endowed with understanding

verses.text: Then Hiram king of Tyre wrote a letter in reply to Solomon: "Because the LORD loves His people, He has set you over them as king."

And Hiram added: "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who made the heavens and the earth! He has given King David a {{chokmah|wise}} son with insight and understanding, who will build a temple for the LORD and a royal palace for himself.
So now I am sending you Huram-abi, a skillful man endowed with creativity.

He is the son of a woman from the daughters of Dan, and his father is a man of Tyre. He is skilled in work with gold and silver, bronze and iron, stone and wood, purple, blue, and crimson yarn, and fine linen. He is experienced in every kind of engraving and can execute any design that is given him. He will work with your craftsmen and with those of my lord, your father David.
Now let my lord send to his servants the wheat, barley, olive oil, and wine he promised.
We will cut logs from Lebanon, as many as you need, and we will float them to you as rafts by sea down to Joppa. Then you can take them up to Jerusalem."
Solomon numbered all the foreign men in the land of Israel following the census his father David had conducted, and there were found to be 153,600 in all.
Solomon made 70,000 of them porters, 80,000 stonecutters in the mountains, and 3,600 supervisors.

shem.gloss: Name. Solomon builds not a house for God to be confined in, but a house for God's shem, His revealed character and presence, to dwell there, repeated throughout chapters 2 and 6 as the theological key to what the temple is and is not.

bayit.gloss: House. The word runs through the chapter for both the temple, God's house, and Solomon's own royal palace, deliberately paired so that the reader notices Solomon is building two houses, and only one of them could ever be great enough, and even that one cannot contain its true occupant.

chokmah.gloss: Wisdom, skill. Hiram praises David's son as a wise son with insight and understanding, and sends a craftsman, Huram-abi, endowed with the same kind of skilled understanding to work with gold, silver, bronze, and every craft, showing that the wisdom God gave Solomon in chapter 1 now extends even to Israel's foreign partners recognizing and serving it.

shamayim.gloss: Heaven, heavens. Before a single stone is cut, Solomon confesses that the shamayim, even the highest heavens, cannot contain God, so the temple he is about to build can never be more than a place to burn sacrifice before Him, a truth he will repeat and expand in his dedicatory prayer, chapter 6.

basic.context: Before construction begins, Solomon organizes his workforce and writes to Hiram, the king of Tyre who had supplied his father David with cedar. Solomon's letter is remarkable for what it confesses up front, our God is greater than all gods, and the heavens themselves cannot contain Him, so this house can only ever be a place to offer sacrifice, never a home that holds God captive. Hiram replies with genuine praise for the God of Israel and sends timber, provisions, and a master craftsman, Huram-abi, to help build it.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative describing a specific building project and diplomatic exchange; it is not a manual for construction projects today. What is enduring is the theology Solomon states before he builds anything: no structure, however great, can contain the infinite God, and even genuine worship spaces exist only as places to meet with Him, not to house Him.
basic.originalLanguages: Solomon writes of building a bayit, a house, for the shem, the Name, of the LORD, language that frames the whole project around God's revealed presence rather than His physical containment. He confesses that even the shamayim, the highest heavens, cannot hold God, and Hiram in turn recognizes the chokmah, wisdom, God has given Solomon, sending a craftsman of matching skill to help build the house.
basic.typology: The temple built to house God's Name yet unable to contain Him anticipates the incarnation, when the Word who filled heaven and earth was pleased to dwell in a human body, and later the church, described as a spiritual house or temple built of living stones. Huram-abi, a skilled craftsman from a mixed Israelite and Tyrian household, foreshadows the gathering of the nations into the service and worship of the true temple, Christ and His people.
basic.christ: Solomon confesses that no house, however great, can contain the God of heaven, a truth answered fully when the eternal Word became flesh and dwelt among us, John 1:14, the true temple in whom the fullness of deity dwells bodily, Colossians 2:9. Where Solomon needed a foreign king's help to gather cedar and craftsmen, Christ Himself is both the builder and the cornerstone of a greater house, His church, gathered from every nation, 1 Peter 2:4-6.
basic.god: God is so vast that even the highest heavens cannot contain Him, yet He is willing to have His Name dwell among His people in a house built by human hands. He is a God whose greatness even outsiders like Hiram can recognize and praise, and He supplies the skill, materials, and cooperation needed to accomplish what He has purposed, often through unexpected partners.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Kings 5 gives the parallel account of Solomon's correspondence with Hiram. Acts 7:48 to 50 echoes Solomon's own confession that the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands. Ephesians 2:19 to 22 describes believers being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit. And 1 Peter 2:4 to 6 calls the church living stones built into a spiritual house.
basic.oneStory: Even before the temple rises, its theology is already settled: God cannot be contained by any house, yet He graciously allows His Name to dwell among His people. Hiram's willing help from outside Israel previews the gathering of the nations into the worship of the true God, a gathering that comes to full flower in Christ, the true temple, and His church, a house built of living stones from every people.

context.literary:
The chapter is built almost entirely from a single exchange of letters, and the Chronicler lets the correspondence carry nearly all of the theology. Solomon's message, verses three through ten, opens with a request modeled on a precedent, do for me as you did for my father, before pivoting, without transition, into a confession about the nature of God that has nothing to do with logistics, the heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain Him. A business letter becomes a doctrinal statement in the space of two verses, and the request for timber and craftsmen that follows is framed by that confession rather than the other way around.

Hiram's reply mirrors the same shape in miniature. He opens with praise of the LORD who made heaven and earth, verse twelve, before descending to the practical matters of Huram-abi's skills and the logistics of floating logs down to Joppa. The two letters answer each other point for point, Solomon's house for my father becomes Hiram's your father David, Solomon's confession of God's greatness becomes Hiram's blessing of that same God, so that even the diplomatic form of the chapter performs the mutual recognition its content describes.

The closing census, verses seventeen and eighteen, deliberately repeats the numbers already given in verse two almost word for word, an inclusio that brackets the entire negotiation and signals that preparation, not yet construction, is now complete.
context.historical:
Tyre's relationship with Israel's throne was not new. 1 Chronicles 14:1 already records Hiram sending cedar and craftsmen to build David's own house decades earlier, so Solomon's opening line, do for me as you did for my father, appeals to an established royal friendship rather than opening a cold negotiation. Phoenician Tyre controlled the cedar forests of Lebanon and had no comparable agricultural hinterland of its own, which is precisely why Solomon's payment is not silver but enormous quantities of wheat, barley, wine, and oil, a trade of food for timber that made sense for a coastal city dependent on imported grain.

The workforce Solomon numbers in verse seventeen, a hundred and fifty three thousand six hundred foreign residents, is explained more fully later in the book, 2 Chronicles 8:7-8, as descendants of the Canaanite peoples who had survived the conquest and remained in the land, a detail the Chronicler assumes his readers already know from Joshua and Judges. Huram-abi's mixed parentage, a Danite mother and a Tyrian father, verse fourteen, reflects the ordinary reality of intermarriage and trade along Israel's northern border, and his specific skills, work in metal, stone, wood, and dyed textiles, match almost item for item the description of Bezalel and Oholiab centuries earlier, suggesting the Chronicler wants this craftsman recognized as their historical and vocational heir.
context.canonical:
The parallel account in 1 Kings 5 records the same correspondence but places Solomon's confession that heaven cannot contain God, 1 Kings 8:27, only in the later dedicatory prayer instead. The Chronicler moves that confession forward, planting it at the very start of construction rather than waiting until the building is finished, so that his readers meet the doctrine before they meet a single measurement of gold or bronze.

Deuteronomy's own Name theology stands behind Solomon's language throughout the letter. Moses had promised that the LORD would choose a place to put His Name and make His dwelling there, Deuteronomy 12:5 and 12:11, language Solomon now claims is being fulfilled in his own generation. The chapter therefore functions as a hinge between Torah's centuries old promise and its concrete, datable fulfillment in Jerusalem.

Stephen's speech in Acts 7:48-50 later echoes almost exactly Solomon's confession here, that the Most High does not dwell in houses made with hands, applying words first spoken about cedar and gold to a far larger argument about the temple's own limits before the risen Christ. What Solomon confessed as true even of his own finished temple, Stephen uses two centuries after its final destruction to explain why God was never confined to it in the first place.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The Chronicler wants his readers, who have watched Solomon's temple reduced to rubble and its treasures carried to Babylon, to see that the building itself was never the real point even while it was still standing. By putting a confession of God's transcendence into Solomon's mouth before a single stone is cut, the author teaches that the temple's builders themselves understood its limits from day one; its loss, therefore, is not evidence that God abandoned His promise but a return to the very truth Solomon confessed at the start. He also wants his readers to notice, through Hiram's blessing, that recognition of Israel's God was never limited to Israelites, preparing a community rebuilding among suspicious neighbors to expect that some outsiders, like Hiram, will bless rather than oppose what they are doing.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The chapter narrates one specific international transaction, cedar for wheat, craftsmen for provisions, between two particular kings; it gives no rule for how congregations should fund buildings or which nations to partner with today. What is transferable is the theology voiced along the way, that any structure built for worship, however costly, only ever functions as a place to meet God rather than a container for Him, and that skilled craftsmanship offered in His service, whether Huram-abi's engraving or any believer's trade, is itself a form of worship rather than a merely secular activity subordinate to it. Applying Hiram's blessing as though every business partnership with an outsider will yield the same friendly outcome would overreach the text, which records one gracious exchange rather than promising a universal pattern of cooperation.

debates.question: Why does Solomon relocate his confession that heaven cannot contain God, verse six, to the start of construction rather than leaving it, as 1 Kings does, for the dedication prayer after the temple is finished?

views.label: A deliberate theological framing device
views.case: By placing the confession before any material is gathered, the Chronicler ensures that every gold overlay and bronze basin described in the chapters that follow is read through a lens already established, nothing built here could ever contain God, guarding his readers in advance against mistaking size or splendor for divine presence.

views.label: A natural feature of an already condensed source
views.case: The Chronicler regularly compresses and rearranges material from Kings to fit his own narrative rhythm; the appearance of this confession earlier may simply reflect a different arrangement of shared source material available to both authors rather than a pointed theological rearrangement.

debates.bearing: Even readers who favor the second view agree the effect is the same, the confession now governs the reader's experience of the whole building account that follows, whatever the cause of its placement.

debates.question: Is Hiram's praise of the LORD in verse twelve genuine worship or diplomatic courtesy?

views.label: Genuine, if partial, recognition
views.case: Ancient Near Eastern kings did not typically credit a neighboring nation's god with making heaven and earth merely as flattery; Hiram's specific wording goes beyond polite formula and anticipates the fuller confession the queen of Sheba will make in chapter nine, suggesting a real, growing reputation for the LORD among surrounding nations.

views.label: Standard royal courtesy with the Chronicler's own theological point layered on top
views.case: Ancient diplomatic letters conventionally invoked blessings from whichever god the addressee served, so Hiram's words may reflect nothing more than expected court etiquette; what matters for the Chronicler's purpose is not Hiram's private convictions but that the words appear in the text at all, letting a foreign voice confirm what Solomon has just confessed.

debates.bearing: Either reading serves the same narrative function, a king with no covenant obligation to Israel's God nonetheless speaks true things about Him, foreshadowing every later scene in Chronicles where an outsider recognizes what Israel already knows.

study.originalLanguages:
Four features of the Hebrew reward attention beyond shem, bayit, shamayim, and chokmah already named. Solomon's language for God's dwelling place draws directly on the Name theology of Deuteronomy, which repeatedly promises that the LORD will choose a place to put His Name there, Deuteronomy 12:5, or to make His Name dwell there, Deuteronomy 12:11. The verb behind dwell, shakan, is the same root that gives mishkan, tabernacle, and later rabbinic Hebrew would develop it into shekhinah, the more technical term for God's manifest presence; Solomon's letter, without using either noun, is already living inside that verbal world, describing a house for God's Name rather than for God's body.

The workforce itself carries its own vocabulary. Those the BSB renders porters, verse two, translate a Hebrew phrase built on sabal, to bear a heavy load; the same verb sabal describes the Suffering Servant centuries later, who has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows, Isaiah 53:4, and who shall bear their iniquities, Isaiah 53:11. The word used for common manual labor under Solomon becomes, in Isaiah, the word for redemptive suffering carried on behalf of others, a striking reuse of ordinary vocabulary for an extraordinary purpose.

The stonecutters of the same verse render chotsevim, from chatsab, to hew or cut stone, the identical verb used of Moses cutting two tablets of stone at the LORD's command, Exodus 34:1; the craft that shapes building stones in Solomon's quarries is, in Exodus, the very verb used for shaping the tablets of the covenant itself.

Finally, Hiram's description of Huram-abi as endowed with creativity or understanding, verse thirteen, echoes the standard biblical formula for skilled temple craftsmen, chakam lev, wise of heart, first used of Bezalel's whole team of artisans in the wilderness, every wise-hearted man in whose heart the LORD had put wisdom, Exodus 35:10 and 31:6. Hiram, a foreign king with no covenant claim on that language, nonetheless describes his own craftsman with the very idiom Israel's own Scriptures reserve for those specially equipped to build for God, whether he knew the connection or simply used the natural word for exceptional skill. Each of these terms shows the same pattern: ordinary vocabulary for labor, craft, and dwelling carries theological freight throughout the Hebrew Bible that a single English word cannot always preserve, which is part of why a slow, attentive reading of even a preparatory chapter like this one repays the effort.

typology.type: The house built for God's Name that even the highest heavens cannot contain, verse six
typology.fulfillment: The confession finds its full answer in the incarnation, when the Word who filled heaven and earth was pleased to tabernacle among us in a human body, John 1:14, and later in the church, built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit, Ephesians 2:22. The type still falls short at Solomon's own admission, since his house was built by human skill and stood for less than four centuries before its destruction, while the dwelling Christ builds cannot be shaken and never falls, Hebrews 12:27-28.

typology.type: The porters who bear the temple's heavy loads before a stone is even cut, verse two
typology.fulfillment: The same Hebrew verb, sabal, describes the Servant of Isaiah 53 who bears griefs and carries sorrows not his own, Isaiah 53:4, 11, a burden borne for others rather than for wages. Solomon's porters carried stone and timber for pay under compulsion; Christ carries the actual weight of sin willingly, once, and the correspondence is one of contrast as much as pattern, ordinary conscripted labor set beside a voluntary, unrepeatable act of bearing what no laborer could ever be hired to carry.

typology.type: Huram-abi, a craftsman of mixed Israelite and Tyrian descent called wise of heart to build God's house, verses thirteen and fourteen
typology.fulfillment: His presence anticipates the gathering of the nations into the work and worship of the true temple, Christ and His people, drawn from Jew and Gentile alike into one household, Ephesians 2:19-21. Where Huram-abi remained an outside contributor, skilled but not himself an Israelite worshiper by birthright, believers from every nation are built into the house itself as living stones, not merely hired to construct it, 1 Peter 2:5.

typology.type: Hiram's blessing of the LORD who made heaven and earth, spoken by a king outside the covenant, verse twelve
typology.fulfillment: Anticipates the confession Paul expects even outsiders to make when they see God genuinely at work among His gathered people, falling on their faces to worship and declaring that God is certainly among you, 1 Corinthians 14:24-25. Hiram's single moment of recognition, however sincere, remained occasional and external; the New Testament pictures a permanent ingathering of the nations into the worship Hiram could only bless from outside.

study.christ:
Solomon's confession that even the highest heavens cannot contain God, verse six, points forward to Christ along two distinct lines. First, by way of astonishing contrast, the God too vast for any house was, in the fullness of time, content to be contained in the womb of a young woman and then in an ordinary human body, the Word become flesh who tabernacled among us, John 1:14. What Solomon rightly declared impossible for architecture, God accomplished anyway, not by shrinking Himself into a building but by taking on a nature that could walk, eat, sleep, and finally suffer and die, so that Paul can write of Christ that in Him all the fullness of deity dwells bodily, Colossians 2:9, using the same root idea, dwelling, that governs Solomon's whole letter.

Second, by way of the church, the house being built now. Peter takes up exactly this temple language and reapplies it to living stones, believers themselves being built into a spiritual house, 1 Peter 2:5, with Christ as the cornerstone that governs the whole structure, 1 Peter 2:6. Where Solomon needed to import both timber and a skilled craftsman from a foreign king because Israel could not supply everything the project required, Christ requires no import; He is Himself the builder, 1 Corinthians 3:11, and the material, gathering the living stones of His church from Jew and Tyrian alike into a single house that, unlike cedar and gold, cannot be looted or burned.

Even the specific craftsman sent, Huram-abi, of mixed Israelite and Gentile parentage, working with his own hands in gold, silver, bronze, and dyed fabric, anticipates a house built from more than one people. Solomon's temple absorbed a Gentile's skill without absorbing Gentiles into its worship on equal footing, a limitation the wall of the temple courts would later make literal. Christ's house has torn down exactly that wall, so that Gentile and Jew together are being built into a dwelling place for God, Ephesians 2:14, 2:22, a temple no single nation's craftsmen could ever have finished alone.
study.god:
God is shown here as a God whose transcendence and whose willingness to dwell among His people are not in tension but are held together in a single confession. Solomon does not first prove God's greatness and then, as an afterthought, allow for His nearness; he states in the very same paragraph that the highest heavens cannot contain Him and that a house should still be built for sacrifice before Him, verse six, refusing to let either truth cancel the other.

God is also shown to be recognizable even by those outside His covenant. Hiram, with no obligation to Israel's God and no history of worshiping Him, nonetheless identifies Him correctly as the maker of heaven and earth, verse twelve, and credits Him, not merely court flattery toward Solomon, with giving David a wise son. Scripture elsewhere insists that what can be known about God is evident even to those who have not received His covenant, and this chapter offers a concrete, narrative example of exactly that kind of recognition happening in real time, centuries before it becomes a settled doctrine.

God is also a God who supplies what His people lack through means they did not expect. Israel had stonecutters and porters in abundance but no comparable tradition of fine metalwork and dyed textile engraving; God's provision for the temple comes not by multiplying Israelite skill directly but by moving a foreign king's heart to send exactly the craftsman needed, work God accomplishes through ordinary international trade and existing royal friendship rather than through a new miracle. And God is shown, in Solomon's own words, to be worthy of a house built as great and wonderful as human resources allow, verse nine, even while that same house is confessed to be radically inadequate to His actual size, a paradox this passage never tries to resolve, only to state plainly and let stand.

crossReferences.note: The fuller parallel account of Solomon's correspondence with Hiram and the arrangement for cedar, craftsmen, and provisions, arranged in a slightly different order and without the explicit confession of God's transcendence that the Chronicler places at the heart of Solomon's own letter.

Hiram had already sent cedar, masons, and carpenters to build David's own house years earlier, the established royal friendship Solomon now appeals to when he asks Hiram to do for me as you did for my father David.

Moses promises that the LORD will choose a place to put His Name there and make His dwelling among His people, the centuries old promise Solomon's letter treats as now reaching its concrete, datable fulfillment in Jerusalem.

Bezalel and Oholiab, filled with the Spirit of God for skill in every craft, supplied the original pattern for Huram-abi's own gifting, so that Solomon's temple craftsman stands in a direct vocational line reaching back to the wilderness tabernacle's own builders.

The Servant who bears griefs and carries sorrows, and who shall bear the iniquities of many, uses the same Hebrew verb, sabal, applied to Solomon's conscripted porters, turning a word for ordinary forced labor into the vocabulary of substitutionary suffering.

Stephen echoes the substance of Solomon's own confession, that the Most High does not dwell in houses made with hands, using words first spoken at the start of the temple's construction to explain, centuries after its destruction, why God was never confined to it.

Believers are described as living stones being built into a spiritual house, with Christ as the cornerstone, taking up the very language of construction and craftsmanship this chapter uses of cedar, gold, and bronze and applying it to people gathered from every nation.
Gentile and Jew together are built into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit, the fulfillment of the pattern begun when a Tyrian craftsman first lent his skill to Israel's own house for God's Name.

Paul expects an outsider entering a gathering of believers to fall down and declare that God is certainly among them, the pattern Hiram's own blessing of the LORD in verse twelve anticipates on a smaller, one time scale.

study.oneStory:
This chapter sits at the moment when a promise voiced centuries earlier in the wilderness begins to take physical shape. Moses had told Israel that one day the LORD would choose a single place to put His Name there, Deuteronomy 12:11, without naming when or where; Solomon's letter to Hiram is the first concrete evidence, datable and specific, that the waiting is over and the chosen place is Jerusalem.

Yet the passage refuses to let that fulfillment become an ending in itself. Solomon's own confession, that not even the highest heavens can contain God, plants inside the very moment of fulfillment the seed of its own future obsolescence; a house this size was never going to be the last word on where God dwells. The rest of the Bible's story of dwelling places runs from this admission rather than around it, through the temple's eventual destruction, through the Word made flesh who succeeds where cedar and gold could not, and into a church gathered, like Huram-abi himself, from more than one people.

Hiram's blessing of the LORD, spoken by an outsider before a single stone of the temple is laid, also anticipates a theme the whole Bible keeps developing, that God's reputation and God's welcome were never meant to stop at Israel's border. What begins here as one foreign king's passing recognition becomes, by the end of the story, nations streaming to the light of a city that needs no temple at all, because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22-24, the final and complete answer to Solomon's own confession that no house, however great, could ever be great enough.

quiz.q: What did Solomon confess about God even before construction of the temple began?

options.text: That the heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain Him, so the temple could only ever be a place to burn sacrifice before Him.
options.note: Verse 6 records this confession directly, framing the whole project's theology.

options.text: That the temple would be able to fully contain and localize God's presence.
options.note: Solomon explicitly denies this is possible in verse 6.

options.text: That God did not care whether a temple was built at all.
options.note: Solomon clearly regards the temple as important and worth building great and wonderful, verse 9.

options.text: The chapter records no theological reflection at all.
options.note: Verses 5-6 contain explicit theological confession.

quiz.q: Who did Solomon write to for help building the temple, and why?

options.text: Hiram king of Tyre, because he had previously supplied cedar and skilled craftsmen to Solomon's father David.
options.note: Verse 3 explicitly recalls Hiram's earlier help to David as the basis for Solomon's request.

options.text: Pharaoh of Egypt, for gold and silver.
options.note: The chapter's request is to Hiram of Tyre for timber and craftsmen, not to Egypt for precious metals.

options.text: The king of Aram, for horses and chariots.
options.note: This chapter concerns Hiram of Tyre and building materials, not Aram or military equipment.

options.text: No one; Solomon built the temple using only Israelite labor and materials.
options.note: The chapter explicitly describes Solomon's request to Hiram and the arrival of Huram-abi.

quiz.q: How did Hiram respond to Solomon's request?

options.text: He blessed the LORD, praised Solomon's God-given wisdom, and sent timber along with the skilled craftsman Huram-abi.
options.note: Verses 11-16 record Hiram's blessing, praise, and practical provision.

options.text: He refused, saying Tyre owed Israel nothing.
options.note: The opposite occurs; Hiram willingly agrees and sends help.

options.text: He demanded that Solomon convert to the gods of Tyre first.
options.note: No such demand appears; Hiram instead praises the LORD, the God of Israel.

options.text: He sent no reply at all.
options.note: Verses 11-16 record a detailed reply and provision from Hiram.

quiz.q: What does Hiram's praise of the LORD in verse 12 suggest?

options.text: Even a foreign king recognized and praised the greatness of Israel's God and the wisdom He had given Solomon.
options.note: Verse 12 has Hiram blessing the LORD who made heaven and earth and praising David's wise son.

options.text: That Hiram secretly worshiped the LORD as his only god from birth.
options.note: The text records his praise but does not claim this level of prior devotion; it is presented as recognition prompted by what he sees in Solomon and Israel.

options.text: That Hiram mocked Solomon's request.
options.note: Hiram's words are praise and blessing, not mockery.

options.text: The verse contains no reference to God at all.
options.note: Verse 12 explicitly names the LORD, the God of Israel, who made the heavens and the earth.

quiz.q: How does Solomon's confession that heaven cannot contain God point forward in Scripture?

options.text: To the incarnation, when the eternal Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and to the church built as God's dwelling place by the Spirit.
options.note: John 1:14 and Ephesians 2:19-22 both develop this trajectory from a house for God's Name to God dwelling among His people directly.

options.text: To the idea that no temple or place of worship is ever needed.
options.note: Solomon still builds the temple as a genuine place to meet God; the point is that it does not contain Him, not that such places are pointless.

options.text: To a complete rejection of all religious buildings in the New Testament.
options.note: The New Testament reinterprets the temple through Christ and the church rather than simply rejecting sacred space altogether.

options.text: It has no connection to anything in the New Testament.
options.note: Acts 7:48-50 and other texts directly echo this very confession.

questions: Solomon confessed God's greatness before he had built anything. Where in your life do you need to remember God's greatness before tackling a task, rather than after?
Hiram, an outsider, recognized and praised the God of Israel. Who around you might be watching your life and drawing conclusions about God, whether you realize it or not?
Solomon relied on skilled help from beyond Israel to build God's house. Where do you need to humbly accept help from others rather than trying to do everything alone?
The temple could never contain God, yet it was still worth building well. How do you hold together reverence for God's greatness with careful, excellent effort in the tasks He gives you?
Christ is described as a greater temple, and His church as a house of living stones. How does knowing you are part of that living house shape how you see your own part in the church this week?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote notes that cypress may also be rendered pine, juniper, or fir, and that algum is likely a variant of the almug wood mentioned in 1 Kings 10:11.

The measures given, 20,000 cors of wheat and barley and 20,000 baths of wine and oil, are enormous quantities, roughly thousands of tons and tens of thousands of gallons, underscoring the scale of Solomon's provision for Hiram's workers.
Huram-abi's name is a variant of Hiram; abi may function as an honorific title, master or my father, rather than a strict patronymic, distinguishing the craftsman from the king who shares his name.
